title: 1 Kings 20:1–12
context: Ben Hadad of Syria and thirty-two allied kings besiege Samaria and demand Ahab’s wealth and family. Ahab first submits, then, on the elders’ counsel, refuses the second, harsher demand, and Ben Hadad prepares to attack.

verses.text: Ben Hadad the king of Syria gathered all his army together; and there were thirty-two kings with him, with horses and chariots. He went up and besieged Samaria, and fought against it.
verses.arminianNotes: Ben Hadad of Syria, with thirty-two allied kings, besieges Samaria. Arminian readers see the narrative setting Israel’s king in grave danger, a setting in which God will show his power to a king who had largely turned from him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s providence at work behind the movements of nations. Many in this tradition caution against identifying this Ben Hadad with certainty, since the name appears for more than one Syrian ruler.

verses.text: He sent messengers into the city to Ahab king of Israel and said to him, “Ben Hadad says,
verses.arminianNotes: Ben Hadad sends messengers into the city to Ahab. Arminian readers see the narrative building tension through diplomatic exchanges before any battle, showing how pressure is applied to Israel’s king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the story unfold through the words of messengers. The narrator lets the demands speak for themselves, so readers can weigh Ahab’s responses as they come.

verses.text: ‘Your silver and your gold are mine. Your wives also and your children, even the best, are mine.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Ben Hadad claims, “Your silver and your gold are mine. Your wives also and your children.” Arminian readers see arrogant overreach from a ruler who trusts his military strength rather than any higher authority.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a proud claim that God will soon overturn. The demand sets up the contrast between human boasting and the LORD’s power announced later in the chapter.

verses.text: The king of Israel answered, “It is according to your saying, my lord, O king. I am yours, and all that I have.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab answers, “It is according to your saying, my lord, O king. I am yours, and all that I have.” Arminian readers see a weak king submitting quickly, perhaps hoping to end the siege; the text does not state his reasoning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note Ahab’s ready submission. Many in this tradition observe that the narrative does not explain whether the reply is sincere or a diplomatic formula, and they avoid inferring a motive.

verses.text: The messengers came again and said, “Ben Hadad says, ‘I sent indeed to you, saying, “You shall deliver me your silver, your gold, your wives, and your children;
verses.arminianNotes: The messengers return: “Ben Hadad says, ‘I sent indeed to you’” demanding silver, gold, wives, and children. Arminian readers see the enemy pressing further after an initial concession, a common pattern of escalating demands.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the demands growing harsher. The repeated message shows how appeasement invites more pressure, preparing for the moment when Ahab finally refuses.

verses.text: but I will send my servants to you tomorrow about this time, and they will search your house and the houses of your servants. Whatever is pleasant in your eyes, they will put it in their hand, and take it away.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Ben Hadad threatens to send servants to search the houses and take “Whatever is pleasant in your eyes.” Arminian readers see a demand that moves from tribute to plunder of the whole city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the escalation from Ahab’s household to his servants’ houses. The demand now affects the people, which leads Ahab to consult the elders in the next verse.

verses.text: Then the king of Israel called all the elders of the land, and said, “Please notice how this man seeks mischief; for he sent to me for my wives, and for my children, and for my silver, and for my gold; and I didn’t deny him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab tells the elders, “Please notice how this man seeks mischief.” Arminian readers see the king seeking counsel from the community’s leaders rather than acting alone in a crisis.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Ahab turning to the elders. Readers in this tradition note that the narrative records Ahab’s consultation without yet mentioning any inquiry of the LORD.

verses.text: All the elders and all the people said to him, “Don’t listen, and don’t consent.”
verses.arminianNotes: The elders and people say, “Don’t listen, and don’t consent.” Arminian readers see the community taking responsibility and urging resistance to an unjust demand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the people’s counsel stiffening the king’s resolve. The united response of elders and people shows that the threat is felt by the whole city.

verses.text: Therefore he said to the messengers of Ben Hadad, “Tell my lord the king, ‘All that you sent for to your servant at the first I will do, but this thing I cannot do.’ ” The messengers departed and brought him back the message.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab replies, “All that you sent for to your servant at the first I will do, but this thing I cannot do.” Arminian readers see a limited but real refusal after consulting the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Ahab drawing a line. The careful wording concedes the first demand while rejecting the second, keeping diplomacy alive while resisting plunder.

verses.text: Ben Hadad sent to him, and said, “The gods do so to me, and more also, if the dust of Samaria will be enough for handfuls for all the people who follow me.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ben Hadad swears by “The gods” that Samaria’s dust will not be enough for handfuls for his followers. Arminian readers see a boastful oath that claims victory before the battle is fought.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a pagan king invoking his gods in arrogance. The boast sets up a contest the narrator will frame as one between human pride and the LORD.

verses.text: The king of Israel answered, “Tell him, ‘Don’t let him who puts on his armor brag like he who takes it off.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab answers, “Don’t let him who puts on his armor brag like he who takes it off.” Arminian readers see a proverb reminding the boastful that outcomes are not settled before the fight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see wisdom in the saying, even on Ahab’s lips. Readers in this tradition note how the proverb fits the chapter’s theme that victory belongs to the LORD, not to the proud.

verses.text: When Ben Hadad heard this message as he was drinking, he and the kings in the pavilions, he said to his servants, “Prepare to attack!” So they prepared to attack the city.
verses.arminianNotes: Ben Hadad, drinking with the kings in the pavilions, says, “Prepare to attack!” Arminian readers see carelessness and overconfidence that will contribute to his defeat.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the narrator highlighting Ben Hadad’s drinking. The detail anticipates the next scene, where his self-indulgence contrasts with God’s word of deliverance.
